text: André-Jean-Jacques Deshayes (abbreviated as A.J.J. Deshayes) was a French ballet dancer, choreographer, and ballet master born in Paris on 24 January 1777 and died in Batignolles on 10 December 1846. He was the son of Jacques-Francois Deshayes, the ballet master of the Comédie-Italienne, and began his dance training with his father before studying at the school of the Paris Opera Ballet from 1788, where he made his debut in young child roles. Hired as Principal Dancer by the Opera in 1794 under Pierre Gardel, he toured abroad, notably in Lisbon in 1799 and London the following year. After leaving the Opera in 1802, he spent two years at La Scala in Milan before dancing in Naples and Vienna. Most of his distinguished career was spent at The King's Theatre in London, where he served as principal dancer and choreographer from 1804 to 1842, with interruptions due to the Napoleonic Wars, which required him to return to the continent. During this period, he played a key role in the development of Romantic ballet in Great Britain. Upon retiring in 1842, he returned to Paris to the newly established quarter of Batignolles, where he died at the age of 69. In 1822, he published his work Idées générales sur l'Académie royale de musique, et plus spécialement sur la danse (Paris, La Mongie).
